label: The Golden Section and Phyllotaxis
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 160 to 174 and follows one number, tau equals one plus root five over two, through four settings. We watch it organize a divided segment, a regular pentagon, a logarithmic spiral, and the spiral seed patterns of plants, each time as the same surviving ratio.

label: Extreme and Mean Ratio
notes: The golden section is a rule for cutting a segment, not merely the decimal 1.618. Euclid divides the whole so that whole to larger equals larger to smaller. The midpoint-square construction adds a piece of length one over tau, making the total length exactly tau on a unit base.

label: The Defining Equation
notes: Both equal ratios collapse into one quadratic, tau squared equals tau plus one. Dividing by tau gives tau equals one plus one over tau, a self-reference that unrolls into the all-ones continued fraction. That endless string of ones is why tau is the most slowly approximated of all irrational numbers.

label: Pentagon and Pentagram
notes: In a unit-side regular pentagon every diagonal has length tau, so the golden ratio appears before any spiral enters the story. Crossing diagonals cut each other into a unit larger part and a shorter one over tau part, and the inner pentagram repeats the same fivefold geometry at smaller scale.

label: The Golden Rectangle
notes: Because tau equals one plus one over tau, removing a square from a golden rectangle leaves a smaller rectangle similar to the original. Repeating that cut produces a nested infinite family of golden rectangles whose corners spiral inward toward a single accumulation point called the eye of the spiral.

label: The Logarithmic Spiral
notes: Successive rectangle corners obey a fixed similarity: rotate a quarter turn, scale by tau. Iterating this linear map forces a logarithmic relation between radius and angle, giving r equal to mu raised to theta with mu equal to tau to the two over pi. The true curve, not the quarter-circle arc, is this self-similar spiral.

label: Fibonacci Approximants
notes: The all-ones continued fraction means the convergents of tau are exactly ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers. Successive ratios F sub n plus one over F sub n alternately overshoot and undershoot tau while closing in. Cassini's identity provides an integer-level check that the recurrence stays exact at every step.

label: Lucas Numbers and Cassini
notes: The Lucas numbers obey the same recurrence with different seeds and relate to Fibonacci through clean integer identities. Cassini's identity states F sub n minus one times F sub n plus one minus F sub n squared equals minus one to the n, an exact algebraic guard on the whole spiraling geometry.

label: The Golden Angle
notes: A disk phyllotaxis model puts the n-th seed at radius proportional to root n and angle two pi n alpha. The golden choice alpha equal to one over tau squared gives a divergence of about 137.5 degrees, replacing exact angular returns by Fibonacci near-returns so no spokes form and seeds pack evenly.

label: Why Fibonacci Spirals Appear
notes: Because q tau is unusually close to an integer exactly when q is a Fibonacci number, the nearest angular returns of the golden turn happen at Fibonacci offsets. These near-returns are the interlocking clockwise and counterclockwise spiral families, the parastichies, counted in consecutive Fibonacci numbers in sunflowers and pinecones.

label: Phyllotaxis on a Cylinder
notes: Coxeter unrolls a pineapple-like cylinder into a strip and places point n at fractional part of n tau horizontally and n h vertically, with the side edges identified. Straight strip rows wrap into helices. For the standard height the shortest row offsets are five, eight, and thirteen: three consecutive Fibonacci numbers.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: One self-similar invariant runs through the whole chapter. In a segment it is a ratio of three collinear points; in a pentagon, similarity inside the star; in the spiral, a fixed quarter-turn dilation; in phyllotaxis, nearest return modulo one. Naming what survives each similarity is the unifying method.
